blocks.text: The multitude’s claim that God’s judgments are “true and righteous” draws on themes that run through Israel’s story and into the New Testament witness. In that larger biblical setting, justice and righteousness appear in discussions of covenant practice, worship, kingship, wisdom instruction, and prophetic criticism. Revelation 19:1-2 therefore presents judgment not merely as an exercise of power, but in the established biblical vocabulary of divine justice and right judgment.

The marriage of the Lamb and the readiness of his wife have often been considered alongside traditional interpretations of the Song of Songs. Major Jewish traditions have read that Song in terms of God and Israel, while major Christian traditions have read it in terms of Christ and the church or the Word and the soul. These are theological interpretations, however, rather than identities explicitly stated by the Song’s own speakers. They should therefore be distinguished from Revelation 19 itself, which directly names the bridegroom as the Lamb.

Across the surrounding book, Revelation is commonly understood to rework material from Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Its visions consequently participate in a book-wide pattern of presenting their message through scriptural images and language.
